title: The EV Boom Is Happening Without Car Buyers
text:
The most common electric vehicle in your neighborhood might be a blue delivery van. When an Amazon driver swings by with a package, there’s a good chance they will be behind the wheel of an EV. The tech goliath now has at least 50,000 electric vans in its fleet, largely thanks to a partnership with the automaker Rivian. The rest of the online-shopping economy is also turning to EVs: The U.S. Postal Service is rolling out all-electric mail trucks, as are its private-sector rivals, like FedEx. IKEA delivers most of its modular furniture in electric vans and trucks.

 Perhaps you’ve heard that Americans remain stubbornly resistant to buying electric vehicles, even as gas prices have soared this year. Yet the vehicles that surround us are nonetheless shifting toward battery power. It’s not just delivery vans. Thousands of robotaxis are now prowling the streets in more than a dozen cities—and all of them are electric. Order a ride from a human, and you might still end up in an EV: About one in 10 Uber miles in the United States and Canada is now driven by a zero-emissions vehicle. A growing number of businesses, such as AT&T and PepsiCo, are using EVs as company cars, as are governments and police departments . Even Disneyland is swapping out the polluting cars in its famous Autopia attraction for new electric alternatives. The result is a country that is quietly full of shadow EVs that Americans don’t own, but still depend on.

 [ Read: Get ready for Tesla cops ] 

 Corporate America’s affinity for the electric car is not a fixation on the newest technology. It’s a matter of economic reality, Jeremy Michalek, the director of the Vehicle Electrification Group at Carnegie Mellon University, told me. People tend to car-shop with their hearts. You might buy a Toyota because your dad always drove them, or perhaps you’re hesitant to purchase an electric car that needs more than two minutes to refuel because you’re used to the convenience of the gas station. But accountants and fleet managers—technocrats who coordinate an organization’s array of vehicles—do the math. They have an easier time seeing how electric vehicles improve the bottom line.

 Although EVs tend to be more expensive to buy up front, they’re cheaper to operate: In addition to the savings on gas, EVs generally require less maintenance compared with a combustion-powered car and its multitude of moving parts. For a ride-share car that logs three times as many miles as the average vehicle, the math is plain. It doesn’t take long for EVs to overcome the up-front cost and become cheaper than gas cars. In fact, businesses can even make money from driving electric cars, Michalek said. Some modern EVs can sell energy stored in their battery back to the power grid whenever electricity gets expensive—applying the “buy low, sell high” credo of stocks to electrons.

 Plenty of big organizations aren’t ready to ditch the pump for the plug just yet. Battery-powered big rigs have arrived to take on trucking around town, but “long-range trucking—it’s a tough sell,” Michalek said. Electric semitrucks capable of traveling cross-country need enormous batteries, which could take up space and weight that could otherwise go to storing goods. With the help of infrastructure funding passed under President Biden, school districts tried to ditch their gas-powered yellow school buses for all-electric replacements, but many struggled to learn how to maintain a whole new kind of vehicle. Still, enough companies and governments are embracing EVs that they are boosting the industry, Corey Cantor, the research director at the Zero Emission Transportation Association, told me.

 Look no further than Rivian. Although the company is best known for its electric SUVs and trucks, the promise of selling vehicles to other businesses has buoyed Rivian through years of existential peril. Amazon invested heavily to help Rivian develop its commercial van, and now other companies can also buy them. And in March, Rivian scored a billion-dollar deal with Uber to sell the company up to 50,000 R2s that will be deployed as robotaxis. The Uber partnership is “one of the most powerful levers we have for putting electric miles on the road,” R. J. Scaringe, the CEO of Rivian, told me.

 As Silicon Valley races to roll out self-driving cars, tech companies are scooping up lots of EVs. They are especially well suited for the autonomous age: AI is ravenous for electricity, and the same goes for the autonomous systems that allow a car to drive itself; it helps to have a giant battery that can power all that tech while also pushing the vehicle down the highway. Waymo is adding at least 2,000 Jaguar SUVs to power its fleet of self-driving cars. Hyundai just unveiled plans to sell Waymo tens of thousands of EVs for its next generation of self-driving cars. Lucid, another California-based EV start-up, has tried to stabilize its flagging business with robotaxi deals in the United States and Europe. Then there’s Tesla. Even though Elon Musk’s company sells by far the most human-driven EVs in America, he has staked Tesla’s future on self-driving cars. (Last week, Musk said that he will be pulling the plug on the Tesla Cybertruck to free up factory space to make the Cybercab, the robotaxi that Tesla wants to roll out nationwide.)

 Shadow EVs—whether a fully autonomous Waymo or human-driven Amazon van—may eventually help get the rest of the country into the driver’s seat of an electric car. With the exception of Tesla, very few electric carmakers are profitable: Building out the supply chain and infrastructure to manufacture an EV takes many years and billions of dollars. President Trump made a tough situation even more challenging for the auto industry by gutting EV incentives. The business world’s embrace gives car companies the steady revenue stream they need to shore up a nascent industry. Hyundai’s CEO has said that the Waymo deal will help it avert the need to retreat from EVs—unlike many other automakers, who have written off billions in losses. Until more Americans are finally prepared to take the plunge, the future of electric vehicles will rest on fleet managers who are crunching the numbers.
